claim: RBM5 regulates the balance between antagonistic isoforms of the apoptosis-control genes FAS/CD95, Caspase-2 and AID.
source: The multi-domain splicing factor RBM5 regulates the balance between antagonistic isoforms of the apoptosis-control genes FAS/CD95, Caspase-2 and AID.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Bonnal et al., 2008; Fushimi et al., 2008).

claim: An OCRE domain found in RBM5 is important for alternative splicing regulation.
source: An OCRE (OCtamer REpeat of aromatic residues) domain found in RBM5 is important for alternative splicing regulation and mediates interactions with components of the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1E showing that OCRE deletion impairs FAS splicing regulation.

claim: The OCRE domain mediates interactions with components of the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP.
source: An OCRE (OCtamer REpeat of aromatic residues) domain found in RBM5 is important for alternative splicing regulation and mediates interactions with components of the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work cited (Bonnal et al., 2008).

claim: The RBM5 OCRE domain adopts a unique β-sheet fold.
source: We show that the RBM5 OCRE domain adopts a unique β–sheet fold.
evidence: This is supported by NMR structural data presented in Figure 1 and structural statistics in Table 1.

claim: The OCRE domain directly binds to the proline-rich C-terminal tail of the essential snRNP core proteins SmN/B/B'.
source: NMR and biochemical experiments demonstrate that the OCRE domain directly binds to the proline-rich C-terminal tail of the essential snRNP core proteins SmN/B/B'.
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration experiments (Figure 2F,G), GST pull-down assays (Figure 2B,C), and ITC measurements (Table 2).

claim: The NMR structure of an OCRE-SmN peptide complex reveals a specific recognition of poly-proline helical motifs in SmN/B/B'.
source: The NMR structure of an OCRE-SmN peptide complex reveals a specific recognition of poly-proline helical motifs in SmN/B/B'.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure shown in Figure 4 and structural statistics in Table 1.

claim: Mutation of conserved aromatic residues impairs binding to the Sm proteins in vitro.
source: Mutation of conserved aromatic residues impairs binding to the Sm proteins in vitro and compromises RBM5-mediated alternative splicing regulation of FAS/CD95.
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down experiments (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), ITC measurements (Table 2), and yeast two-hybrid assays (Figure 2E).

claim: Mutation of conserved aromatic residues compromises RBM5-mediated alternative splicing regulation of FAS/CD95.
source: Mutation of conserved aromatic residues impairs binding to the Sm proteins in vitro and compromises RBM5-mediated alternative splicing regulation of FAS/CD95.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo splicing assays shown in Figure 1E and Figure 5.

claim: RBM5 OCRE represents a poly-proline recognition domain that mediates critical interactions with the C-terminal tail of the spliceosomal SmN/B/B' proteins in FAS/CD95 alternative splicing regulation.
source: Thus, RBM5 OCRE represents a poly-proline recognition domain that mediates critical interactions with the C-terminal tail of the spliceosomal SmN/B/B' proteins in FAS/CD95 alternative splicing regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined structural, biochemical, and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The spliceosome is a large and dynamic assembly of five small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complexes and more than 150 additional splicing factor proteins.
source: The catalytic steps of pre-mRNA splicing are carried out by the spliceosome, a large and dynamic assembly of five small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complexes and more than 150 additional splicing factor proteins (Wahl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: More than 90% of human multi-exon genes undergo alternative splicing.
source: It is thought that more than 90% of human multi-exon genes undergo alternative splicing (Pan et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The FAS gene encodes a transmembrane signaling protein that stimulates a pro-apoptotic signaling cascade upon binding of the FAS ligand at the cell surface.
source: The FAS gene encodes a transmembrane signaling protein that stimulates a pro-apoptotic signaling cascade upon binding of the FAS ligand at the cell surface (Krammer, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Alternatively spliced FAS transcripts that exclude exon 6 encode a soluble Fas isoform that lacks the transmembrane domain.
source: Alternatively spliced FAS transcripts that exclude exon 6 encode a soluble Fas isoform that lacks the transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Cheng et al., 1994; Cascino et al., 1995).

claim: The soluble Fas isoform can be secreted outside of the cell where it sequesters the FAS ligand and inhibits downstream activation of apoptosis.
source: This soluble isoform can be secreted outside of the cell where it sequesters the FAS ligand and inhibits downstream activation of apoptosis (Cheng et al., 1994; Cascino et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RBM5 regulates FAS splicing by promoting skipping of exon 6.
source: The multi-domain RNA-binding protein 5 (RBM5) regulates FAS splicing by promoting skipping of exon 6 (Bonnal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: RBM5 is a 92 kDa, multi-domain protein with an arginine-serine (RS)-rich region, two RNA Recognition Motifs (RRM1 and RRM2), two Zinc-Finger domains (ZF1 and ZF2), a C-terminal OCtamer REpeat (OCRE) domain in addition to a glycine patch, and KEKE repeats.
source: RBM5 is a 92 kDa, multi-domain protein with an arginine-serine (RS)-rich region, two RNA Recognition Motifs (RRM1 and RRM2), two Zinc-Finger domains (ZF1 and ZF2), a C-terminal OCtamer REpeat (OCRE) domain (Callebaut and Mornon, 2005) in addition to a glycine patch, and KEKE (lysine/glutamate) repeats (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: RBM5 belongs to the family of RNA Binding Motif (RBM) proteins, including RBM6 and RBM10.
source: It belongs to the family of RNA Binding Motif (RBM) proteins, including RBM6 and RBM10, which share a similar domain organization with RBM5 and have 30% and 50% amino acid identity, respectively (Sutherland et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: RBM6 and RBM10 share a similar domain organization with RBM5 and have 30% and 50% amino acid identity, respectively.
source: It belongs to the family of RNA Binding Motif (RBM) proteins, including RBM6 and RBM10, which share a similar domain organization with RBM5 and have 30% and 50% amino acid identity, respectively (Sutherland et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The RBM5 and RBM6 genes are located in a chromosomal region 3p21.3, which is frequently deleted in heavy smokers and lung cancers.
source: The RBM5 (also known as H37 and LUCA-15) and RBM6 genes are located in a chromosomal region 3p21.3, which is frequently deleted in heavy smokers and lung cancers (Oh et al., 2002; Zabarovsky et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RBM5 is known to regulate the alternative splicing of apoptosis–related genes, such as FAS and Caspase-2.
source: RBM5 is known to regulate the alternative splicing of apoptosis–related genes, such as FAS and Caspase-2 (Bonnal et al., 2008; Fushimi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RBM5 has been reported to suppress metastasis by modulating the expression of Rac1, β-catenin, collagen and laminin.
source: It has also been reported to suppress metastasis by modulating the expression of Rac1, β-catenin, collagen and laminin (Oh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: RBM5 has been found to be up-regulated in some aggressive forms of breast and ovarian cancers.
source: However, RBM5 has also been found to be up-regulated in some aggressive forms of breast and ovarian cancers (Oh et al., 1999; Rintala-Maki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RBM5 inhibits mature spliceosome formation by blocking association of the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP complex after the splice sites flanking exon 6 have been recognized by U1 and U2 snRNPs.
source: In the regulation of FAS alternative splicing, RBM5 inhibits mature spliceosome formation by blocking association of the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP complex (in complex B) after the splice sites flanking exon 6 have been recognized by U1 and U2 snRNPs (Bonnal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The OCRE domain of RBM5 interacts with components of the tri-snRNP and is essential for the function of RBM5 in regulating FAS splicing.
source: Moreover, it was shown that the OCRE domain of RBM5 interacts with components of the tri-snRNP and is essential for the function of RBM5 in regulating FAS splicing (Bonnal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data in Figures 1E, 2, and 5.

claim: OCRE domains were identified by bioinformatic sequence analysis as a tandem of five imperfect octameric repeat sequences with triplets of aromatic residues.
source: OCRE domains, which are present in different proteins in various organisms (Xiao et al., 2013), were identified by bioinformatic sequence analysis as a tandem of five imperfect octameric repeat sequences with triplets of aromatic residues (Callebaut and Mornon, 2005), expected to predominantly adopt β-strand secondary conformation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: OCRE domains were expected to predominantly adopt β-strand secondary conformation.
source: OCRE domains, which are present in different proteins in various organisms (Xiao et al., 2013), were identified by bioinformatic sequence analysis as a tandem of five imperfect octameric repeat sequences with triplets of aromatic residues (Callebaut and Mornon, 2005), expected to predominantly adopt β-strand secondary conformation.
evidence: This is a prediction from bioinformatic analysis, supported by citation and confirmed by NMR data in Figure 1.

claim: Sm proteins are core components of most spliceosomal snRNPs and form a heptameric ring composed of SmD1, SmD2, SmF, SmE, SmG, SmD3 and SmN/B/B'.
source: Sm proteins are core components of most spliceosomal snRNPs and form a heptameric ring composed of SmD1, SmD2, SmF, SmE, SmG, SmD3 and SmN/B/B', which jointly recognize the uridine-rich Sm site RNA motif in U1, U2, U4 and U5 snRNAs (Kambach et al., 1999; Will and Lührmann, 2001; Pomeranz Krummel et al., 2009; Weber et al., 2010; Leung et al., 2011; Matera and Wang, 2014; Kondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Sm heptameric ring jointly recognizes the uridine-rich Sm site RNA motif in U1, U2, U4 and U5 snRNAs.
source: Sm proteins are core components of most spliceosomal snRNPs and form a heptameric ring composed of SmD1, SmD2, SmF, SmE, SmG, SmD3 and SmN/B/B', which jointly recognize the uridine-rich Sm site RNA motif in U1, U2, U4 and U5 snRNAs (Kambach et al., 1999; Will and Lührmann, 2001; Pomeranz Krummel et al., 2009; Weber et al., 2010; Leung et al., 2011; Matera and Wang, 2014; Kondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: SmB and SmB' are encoded by two transcript variants from the SNRPB gene.
source: SmB and SmB' are encoded by two transcript variants from the SNRPB gene, while a different gene, highly expressed in brain and heart, encodes the homologous protein SmN (Schmauss et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A different gene, highly expressed in brain and heart, encodes the homologous protein SmN.
source: SmB and SmB' are encoded by two transcript variants from the SNRPB gene, while a different gene, highly expressed in brain and heart, encodes the homologous protein SmN (Schmauss et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SmN/B/B', SmD1, and SmD3 have C-terminal extensions that include symmetrically dimethylated RG repeats.
source: SmN/B/B', SmD1, and SmD3 have C-terminal extensions that include symmetrically dimethylated RG repeats (Brahms et al., 2001; Tripsianes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The SmN/B/B' C-terminal tails contain additional proline-rich sequences.
source: The SmN/B/B' C-terminal tails contain additional proline-rich sequences, where these regions in SmN, SmB and SmB' are 93% homologous (van Dam et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The proline-rich regions in SmN, SmB and SmB' are 93% homologous.
source: The SmN/B/B' C-terminal tails contain additional proline-rich sequences, where these regions in SmN, SmB and SmB' are 93% homologous (van Dam et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The RBM5 OCRE domain binds to the C-terminal proline-rich motifs present in SmB and SmN.
source: Here, we show that the RBM5 OCRE domain binds to the C-terminal proline-rich motifs present in SmB and SmN.
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration experiments (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), ITC measurements (Table 2), and GST pull-down assays (Figure 2B,C).

claim: The structure of the RBM5 OCRE domain adopts a unique β-sheet fold that recognizes the proline-rich C-terminal tails of the SmN/B/B' proteins through aromatic-CH interactions.
source: The structure of the RBM5 OCRE domain adopts a unique β-sheet fold that recognizes the proline-rich C-terminal tails of the SmN/B/B' proteins through aromatic-CH interactions.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR structure shown in Figure 4 and structural analysis.

claim: Disruption of OCRE-SmN interactions by mutations in the OCRE domain decreases the affinity between SmN/B/B' and RBM5 in vitro.
source: We demonstrate that disruption of these interactions by mutations in the OCRE domain or in the proline-rich motifs of its ligands decreases the affinity between SmN/B/B' and RBM5 in vitro and affects alternative splicing regulation of the FAS gene.
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements (Table 2), GST pull-down assays (Figure 2C), and yeast two-hybrid assays (Figure 2E).

claim: Disruption of OCRE-SmN interactions by mutations in the proline-rich motifs of SmN/B/B' decreases the affinity between SmN/B/B' and RBM5 in vitro.
source: We demonstrate that disruption of these interactions by mutations in the OCRE domain or in the proline-rich motifs of its ligands decreases the affinity between SmN/B/B' and RBM5 in vitro and affects alternative splicing regulation of the FAS gene.
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements (Table 2) and splicing assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).

claim: Disruption of OCRE-SmN interactions affects alternative splicing regulation of the FAS gene.
source: We demonstrate that disruption of these interactions by mutations in the OCRE domain or in the proline-rich motifs of its ligands decreases the affinity between SmN/B/B' and RBM5 in vitro and affects alternative splicing regulation of the FAS gene.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo splicing assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: OCRE is a novel protein-protein interaction domain that mediates interactions with the core spliceosome in alternative splicing regulation.
source: Our results demonstrate that OCRE is a novel protein-protein interaction domain that mediates interactions with the core spliceosome in alternative splicing regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined structural, biochemical, and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The OCRE domain spans amino acid residues 451–511 of RBM5.
source: Previous reports (Callebaut and Mornon, 2005) and a multiple sequence alignment of the related splicing factors RBM5, RBM6, and RBM10 indicated that the OCRE domain spans amino acid residues 451–511 of RBM5 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by citation and sequence alignment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NMR chemical shift and 15N relaxation analyses of a construct with a C-terminal extension (451–532, including the KEKE region) did not reveal additional structural elements.
source: NMR chemical shift and 15N relaxation analyses of a construct with a C-terminal extension (451–532, including the KEKE region) did not reveal additional structural elements, suggesting that residues 451–511 indeed define the OCRE fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Residues 451–511 define the OCRE fold.
source: NMR chemical shift and 15N relaxation analyses of a construct with a C-terminal extension (451–532, including the KEKE region) did not reveal additional structural elements, suggesting that residues 451–511 indeed define the OCRE fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is inferred from NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The secondary structure of the RBM5 OCRE domain comprises six β-strands between residues 460 and 505.
source: An analysis of 13C secondary chemical shifts shows that the secondary structure of the RBM5 OCRE domain comprises six β-strands between residues 460 and 505 (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Residues 452–459 preceding β1, and the loops connecting the β-strands are well-structured and not flexible.
source: Notably, residues 452–459 preceding β1, and the loops connecting the β-strands are well-structured and not flexible (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR relaxation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The six β-strands form a twisted β-sheet where aromatic side chains are exposed on opposite surfaces of the β-sheet.
source: The six β–strands form a twisted β–sheet where aromatic side chains are exposed on opposite surfaces of the β–sheet (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in the NMR structure in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The twisted β-sheet of the OCRE domain appears unique.
source: Although the topology of the six antiparallel β-strands is rather simple, the twisted β-sheet of the OCRE domain appears unique.
evidence: This is inferred from structural similarity searches that did not reveal significant structural homologs.

claim: Structural similarity searches with Dali and SSM did not reveal any significant structural homologs (Z-scores <2).
source: Structural similarity searches with Dali (Holm et al., 2008) and SSM (Krissinel and Henrick, 2004) did not reveal any significant structural homologs (Z-scores <2), indicating that the OCRE domain represents a unique fold.
evidence: This is based on computational structural comparison using established methods.

claim: The OCRE domain represents a unique fold.
source: Structural similarity searches with Dali (Holm et al., 2008) and SSM (Krissinel and Henrick, 2004) did not reveal any significant structural homologs (Z-scores <2), indicating that the OCRE domain represents a unique fold.
evidence: This is inferred from structural similarity searches.

claim: The electrostatic surface potential of the OCRE domain is predominantly negatively charged with some hydrophobic patches.
source: The electrostatic surface potential of the OCRE domain is predominantly negatively charged with some hydrophobic patches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), consistent with a potential role in protein–protein interactions and less likely for nucleic acid binding.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The electrostatic surface of the OCRE domain is consistent with a potential role in protein-protein interactions and less likely for nucleic acid binding.
source: The electrostatic surface potential of the OCRE domain is predominantly negatively charged with some hydrophobic patches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), consistent with a potential role in protein–protein interactions and less likely for nucleic acid binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrostatic surface properties shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The YYE mutation (Y495/Y497/E501 to AAK) failed to induce significant levels of FAS exon 6 skipping, similar to the effect of deleting the entire OCRE domain.
source: While the YD mutant had similar activity as the WT protein in promoting Fas exon 6 skipping, the YYE mutation failed to induce significant levels of FAS exon 6 skipping, similar to the effect of deleting the entire OCRE domain (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo splicing assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Replacement of the aromatic tyrosines that are exposed on one surface of the β-sheet to alanine impaired the function of the protein in FAS alternative splicing regulation.
source: Replacement of the aromatic tyrosines that are exposed on one surface of the β-sheet to alanine impaired the function of the protein in FAS alternative splicing regulation, arguing that the tyrosine residues in the surface of the β-sheet are important for the function of the OCRE domain in splicing regulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo splicing assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The tyrosine residues in the surface of the β-sheet are important for the function of the OCRE domain in splicing regulation.
source: Replacement of the aromatic tyrosines that are exposed on one surface of the β-sheet to alanine impaired the function of the protein in FAS alternative splicing regulation, arguing that the tyrosine residues in the surface of the β-sheet are important for the function of the OCRE domain in splicing regulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SmN was among proteins identified by mass-spectrometry, pulled down with GST-OCRE RBM5 from HeLa cell extracts.
source: SmN, a core snRNP protein highly homologous to SmB/B', was among proteins, identified by mass-spectrometry, pulled down with GST-OCRE RBM5 from HeLa cell extracts (Bonnal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: RBM5 was found as an interacting partner in a two-hybrid screen using the C-terminal tail of human SmB as bait.
source: We also found RBM5 as an interacting partner in a two-hybrid screen using the C-terminal tail of human SmB as bait (unpublished results).
evidence: This is based on unpublished experimental data.

claim: SmB and SmB' are ubiquitous.
source: While SmB and SmB' are ubiquitous, SmN is primarily found in neuronal and cardiac cells but has also been found to be expressed in HeLa cells (Sharpe et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SmN is primarily found in neuronal and cardiac cells but has also been found to be expressed in HeLa cells.
source: While SmB and SmB' are ubiquitous, SmN is primarily found in neuronal and cardiac cells but has also been found to be expressed in HeLa cells (Sharpe et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The three SmN/B/B' isoforms have a similar domain architecture, comprising a small globular N-terminal Sm domain and a C-terminal region that is expected to be intrinsically disordered.
source: The three SmN/B/B' isoforms have a similar domain architecture, comprising a small globular N-terminal Sm domain (Kambach et al., 1999) and a C-terminal region that is expected to be intrinsically disordered.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and structural information.

claim: The C-terminal region of SmN/B/B' starts with an arginine-glycine (RG)-rich region at ~residue 90 that harbors symmetrically dimethylated arginine residues.
source: The C-terminal region starts with an arginine-glycine (RG)-rich region at ~residue 90 that harbors symmetrically dimethylated arginine residues, and additionally comprises a 60–70 residue proline-rich region of unknown function beyond residue 167 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and supported by established knowledge.

claim: The C-terminal region of SmN/B/B' comprises a 60–70 residue proline-rich region of unknown function beyond residue 167.
source: The C-terminal region starts with an arginine-glycine (RG)-rich region at ~residue 90 that harbors symmetrically dimethylated arginine residues, and additionally comprises a 60–70 residue proline-rich region of unknown function beyond residue 167 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Recombinant purified GST-RBM5 pulled down in vitro translated SmB.
source: As an initial test, we verified that recombinant purified GST-RBM5, or a derivative containing the C-terminal (OCRE-containing) domain, pulled down in vitro translated SmB, while a GST-fusion of the N-terminal domain of RBM5 did not (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A GST-fusion of the C-terminal (OCRE-containing) domain of RBM5 pulled down in vitro translated SmB.
source: As an initial test, we verified that recombinant purified GST-RBM5, or a derivative containing the C-terminal (OCRE-containing) domain, pulled down in vitro translated SmB, while a GST-fusion of the N-terminal domain of RBM5 did not (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A GST-fusion of the N-terminal domain of RBM5 did not pull down in vitro translated SmB.
source: As an initial test, we verified that recombinant purified GST-RBM5, or a derivative containing the C-terminal (OCRE-containing) domain, pulled down in vitro translated SmB, while a GST-fusion of the N-terminal domain of RBM5 did not (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Recombinant GST-tagged OCRE domain binds SmN in vitro.
source: These experiments demonstrate that recombinant GST-tagged OCRE domain binds SmN in vitro and that the mutations Y479A, Y488A, or Y495A diminish SmN binding (Figure 2C), consistent with the decrease in activity of Y495A in splicing regulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mutations Y479A, Y488A, or Y495A diminish SmN binding.
source: These experiments demonstrate that recombinant GST-tagged OCRE domain binds SmN in vitro and that the mutations Y479A, Y488A, or Y495A diminish SmN binding (Figure 2C), consistent with the decrease in activity of Y495A in splicing regulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mutations Y486A, Y497A and E501K do not significantly impair the interaction between OCRE and SmN.
source: The mutations Y486A, Y497A and E501K do not significantly impair the interaction (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutation of Y495 to tryptophan or phenylalanine did not compromise binding to SmN.
source: Interestingly, mutation of Y495 to tryptophan or phenylalanine did not compromise binding, arguing that an aromatic residue at this position is required for the interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: An aromatic residue at position 495 is required for the interaction between OCRE and SmN.
source: Interestingly, mutation of Y495 to tryptophan or phenylalanine did not compromise binding, arguing that an aromatic residue at this position is required for the interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Yeast-two-hybrid assays demonstrate a robust interaction between RBM5 and the SmB tail.
source: To further characterize these interactions by an independent method, we performed yeast-two-hybrid assays and tested whether the C-terminal tail of SmB binds to different variants of RBM5. These experiments demonstrate a robust interaction between RBM5 and the SmB tail, where the OCRE domain is found to be necessary and sufficient for the interaction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The OCRE domain is necessary and sufficient for the interaction between RBM5 and the SmB tail.
source: These experiments demonstrate a robust interaction between RBM5 and the SmB tail, where the OCRE domain is found to be necessary and sufficient for the interaction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutations of surface-exposed tyrosines to alanine reduce the interaction between RBM5 and SmB tail.
source: Moreover, mutations of surface-exposed tyrosines to alanine reduce the interaction, while mutation to another aromatic amino acid (phenylalanine) maintains the interaction (Figure 2E) as was observed for the full-length SmN protein (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mutation of Y495 to phenylalanine maintains the interaction between RBM5 and SmB tail.
source: Moreover, mutations of surface-exposed tyrosines to alanine reduce the interaction, while mutation to another aromatic amino acid (phenylalanine) maintains the interaction (Figure 2E) as was observed for the full-length SmN protein (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SmN (167–196) and (167–240) bind to RBM5 OCRE with dissociation constants of KD = 195 μM and 41 μM, respectively.
source: SmN (167–196) and (167–240), both of which comprise about one half and the complete proline-rich region, bind to RBM5 OCRE with dissociation constants of KD = 195 μM and 41 μM, respectively, as determined by ITC (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F; Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F and Table 2.

claim: All SmN fragments harboring PRMs utilize the same binding site on the OCRE domain.
source: It is interesting to note that the NMR CSPs observed for the OCRE domain when titrated with a peptide comprising just one proline-rich motif (PRM, residues 219–229) (Figure 2F) or the larger fragments of SmN are very similar (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D). This indicates that all SmN fragments harboring PRMs utilize the same binding site on the OCRE domain.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: The interaction with multiple motifs is enhanced by avidity.
source: Nearly identical spectral changes are induced by the peptide, suggesting that all PRMs contribute to the overall affinity for the OCRE domain. Thus, the interaction with multiple motifs is enhanced by avidity, e.g., interaction of multiple PRMs within the Sm tails provides increased local concentration of PRM ligand motifs and thereby contributes to the significantly higher affinity of Sm-tails compared to a single PRM.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of binding affinities of single PRM peptides versus longer Sm tail constructs.

claim: SmB or SmN contain five to six PRMs harboring three or four consecutive prolines.
source: In order to assess the sequence requirements of PRMs for binding to the OCRE domain, we compared the amino acid sequences of the SmN/B tails (Figure 3A). This analysis reveals the presence of multiple (five to six) PRMs harboring three or four consecutive prolines in SmB or SmN, which are flanked by conserved arginine residues within ±3 residues on either side of the poly-proline motif (Weber et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence analysis in Figure 3A.

claim: PRMs in SmB or SmN are flanked by conserved arginine residues within ±3 residues on either side of the poly-proline motif.
source: This analysis reveals the presence of multiple (five to six) PRMs harboring three or four consecutive prolines in SmB or SmN, which are flanked by conserved arginine residues within ±3 residues on either side of the poly-proline motif (Weber et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence analysis in Figure 3A and supported by citation.

claim: Reducing the number of PRMs significantly decreases the binding affinity to OCRE.
source: Reducing the number or PRMs significantly decreases the binding affinity, consistent with avidity effects and contribution to the overall affinity by the presence of multiple PRMs.
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements shown in Table 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: Replacing four prolines by four alanines has little effect on binding to OCRE.
source: Replacing four prolines by four alanines has little effect. This observation is consistent with the fact that consecutive stretches of alanines adopt a poly-proline type II (PPII) helical conformation, as confirmed by CD spectra (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements (Table 2) and CD spectroscopy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Consecutive stretches of alanines adopt a poly-proline type II (PPII) helical conformation.
source: This observation is consistent with the fact that consecutive stretches of alanines adopt a poly-proline type II (PPII) helical conformation, as confirmed by CD spectra (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is confirmed by CD spectroscopy shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and is established knowledge.

claim: The SmN/B/B' PRMs adopt a PPII helical conformation when bound to the OCRE domain.
source: As the SmN/B/B' PRMs adopt a PPII helical conformation when bound to the OCRE domain (see below), the replacement by four alanines can thus be tolerated to some extent.
evidence: This is shown in the NMR structure of the OCRE-SmN complex in Figure 4.

claim: Charge reversal of two arginines flanking the poly-proline motif on either side significantly decreases the binding affinity to OCRE.
source: Notably, charge reversal of two arginines flanking the poly-proline motif on either side significantly decreases the binding affinity.
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements shown in Table 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: A PPII helical conformation flanked by positively charged arginine residues is specifically recognized by the OCRE domain.
source: These data suggest that a PPII helical conformation flanked by positively charged arginine residues is specifically recognized by the OCRE domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis and binding studies shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: Wild type peptides with three prolines induce smaller CSPs than those with four proline motifs.
source: First, wild type peptides with three prolines induce smaller CSPs than those with four proline motifs and binding saturation is achieved only at higher peptide concentration, indicating a lower affinity.
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PRMs harboring only three consecutive proline residues show 2–3-fold reduced affinity relative to four proline motifs.
source: PRMs harboring only three consecutive proline residues show 2–3-fold reduced affinity relative to four proline motifs.
evidence: This is supported by NMR CSP analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An APAP motif, which disrupts PPII conformations, has a strongly reduced CSP score.
source: Second, an APAP motif, which disrupts PPII conformations, has a strongly reduced CSP score, suggesting that the structure and composition of the PPII are important for interaction.
evidence: This is supported by NMR CSP analysis shown in Figure 3B and CD spectroscopy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The structure and composition of the PPII are important for interaction with OCRE.
source: Second, an APAP motif, which disrupts PPII conformations, has a strongly reduced CSP score, suggesting that the structure and composition of the PPII are important for interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both arginines flanking the PRM motif are important for the interaction with OCRE.
source: Third, both arginines flanking the PRM motif are important for the interaction, as a double charge reversal (R→E) strongly reduces the binding affinity.
evidence: This is supported by NMR CSP analysis shown in Figure 3B and ITC measurements (Table 2).

claim: The arginine residue preceding the PRM appears more important for the interaction than the one located C-terminal to the PRM.
source: Notably, the arginine residue preceding the PRM appears more important for the interaction than the one located C-terminal to the PRM.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A PPII conformation mediated by four consecutive proline residues with flanking positively charged residues is optimal for OCRE binding.
source: Taken together, the analysis shown in Figure 3 indicates that a PPII conformation mediated by four consecutive proline residues with flanking positively charged residues is optimal for OCRE binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined mutational and binding analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The central proline stretch (SmN Pro222-Pro225) of the bound peptide adopts a PPII helix.
source: The structure shows that the central proline stretch (SmN Pro222-Pro225) of the bound peptide adopts a PPII helix (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in the NMR structure in Figure 4.

claim: The PPII conformation is already preformed in the absence of the OCRE domain.
source: The PPII conformation is also indicated by the 13C chemical shifts of the peptide. Considering the large excess of peptide, the chemical shifts largely reflect the unbound state. This indicates that the PPII conformation is already preformed in the absence of the OCRE domain, consistent with our CD data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from NMR chemical shift analysis and supported by CD spectroscopy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The central part of the proline-rich peptide interacts with conserved tyrosine residues in the OCRE domain in strands β3 (Tyr470, Tyr479), β4 (Tyr486, Tyr488) and β5 (Tyr495).
source: The central part of the proline-rich peptide interacts with conserved tyrosine residues in the OCRE domain in strands β3 (Tyr470, Tyr479), β4 (Tyr486, Tyr488) and β5 (Tyr495) (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is shown in the NMR structure in Figure 4A–C.

claim: The side chain of SmN Arg221 interacts with the hydroxyl groups of OCRE Tyr472, Tyr479 and Ser490.
source: The side chain of SmN Arg221, preceding the poly-proline stretch is poised to interact with the hydroxyl groups of OCRE Tyr472, Tyr479 and Ser490 in loop β1-β2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in the NMR structure in Figure 4D.

claim: The side chain of SmN Arg228 can form potential hydrogen bonds with the side chains of Asp481 and Ser484 in the OCRE domain.
source: The side chain of SmN Arg228 can form potential hydrogen bonds with the side chains of Asp481 and Ser484 in the OCRE domain (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in the NMR structure in Figure 4E.

claim: Asp481 and Ser484 are conserved in loop β3-β4 in the OCRE domains of RBM5 and RBM10.
source: Both residues are conserved in loop β3-β4 in the OCRE domains of RBM5 and RBM10 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 1B.

claim: The hydrophobic side chain of SmN Ile227 packs against SmN Pro223 and shields the hydrophobic PPII helix from solvent exposure.
source: In addition, the hydrophobic side chain of SmN Ile227, located C-terminal of the proline-rich motif packs against SmN Pro223, consistent with numerous intermolecular NOEs between the two side chains, and thus shields the hydrophobic PPII helix from solvent exposure (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in the NMR structure in Figure 4C and supported by intermolecular NOEs.

claim: The presence of a preceding Gly226 enables a specific backbone conformation by allowing unusual backbone torsion angles.
source: To enable these contacts involving the Ile227 side chain, the presence of a preceding Gly226, enables a specific backbone conformation by allowing unusual backbone torsion angles.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis of the OCRE-SmN complex.

claim: The specific spacing of the arginine residues to the four-proline-stretch in the SmN ligand defines a unique, unambiguous orientation of the peptide along the OCRE β-sheet surface.
source: Considering the specific spacing of the arginine residues to the four-proline-stretch in the SmN ligand, these interactions define a unique, unambiguous orientation of the peptide along the OCRE β-sheet surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis of the OCRE-SmN complex shown in Figure 4.

claim: The structure of the OCRE domain does not undergo significant conformational changes upon binding to the SmN peptide.
source: The structure of the OCRE domain does not undergo significant conformational changes upon binding to the SmN peptide, with a backbone coordinate r.m.s.d. of 1.7Å between the free and SmN-bound OCRE domain.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of free and bound OCRE structures.

claim: The tyrosine side chains involved in the SmN interaction slightly rearrange to optimize contacts with the proline-rich SmN ligand.
source: However, the tyrosine side chains involved in the SmN interaction slightly rearrange to optimize contacts with the proline-rich SmN ligand.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison of free and bound OCRE structures.

claim: The RBM5 OCRE domain uses an array of tyrosine side chains that are exposed from one side of its β-sheet to recognize a proline-rich motif in a PPII conformation.
source: To summarize, the RBM5 OCRE domain uses an array of tyrosine side chains that are exposed from one side of its β-sheet to recognize a proline-rich motif in a PPII conformation.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Additional specific interactions are mediated by two positively charged side chains flanking the N- and C-terminal sides of the poly-proline helix in the bound SmN peptide.
source: Additional specific interactions are mediated by two positively charged side chains flanking the N- and C-terminal sides of the poly-proline helix in the bound SmN peptide, which in part involve the side chain hydroxyl groups of the exposed tyrosines, thus consistent with the strong conservation of tyrosines in the OCRE domain.
evidence: This is shown in the NMR structure in Figure 4D,E.

claim: The OCRE domain represents a novel proline-rich motif binding domain.
source: These structural insights reveal that the OCRE domain represents a novel proline-rich motif binding domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The Y495A and Y488A mutants show strongly reduced binding to the SmN-derived proline-rich ligands, KD = 172 and 220 μM, respectively, compared to the wild type OCRE domain (KD = 41 μM).
source: Consistent with the structural analysis and the observed effects in splicing regulation, the Y495A and Y488A mutants show strongly reduced binding to the SmN-derived proline-rich ligands, KD = 172 and 220 μM, respectively, compared to the wild type OCRE domain (KD = 41 μM).
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements shown in Table 2.

claim: The Y495F mutation does not strongly affect the SmN interaction (KD = 87 μM).
source: The Y495F mutation does not strongly affect the SmN interaction KD = 87 μM.
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements shown in Table 2.

claim: Substitutions of conserved tyrosines that are involved in SmN interactions (Tyr495 and Tyr497) impair the activity of RBM5 in Fas alternative splicing regulation.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, substitutions of conserved tyrosines that are involved in SmN interactions (Tyr495 and Tyr497) impair the activity of RBM5 in Fas alternative splicing regulation (Figures 5A,C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo splicing assays shown in Figures 1E, 5A,C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutations of aromatic residues, including tyrosines 470, 479, 486 and 488 by alanine compromise the Fas exon 6 skipping activity of RBM5 to different extents.
source: Further mutations of aromatic residues, including tyrosines 470, 479, 486 and 488 by alanine compromise the Fas exon 6 skipping activity of RBM5 to different extents, consistent with the reduced binding of these mutants to SmN-derived proline-rich ligands (see above) and with the location of these residues in the binding pocket for the SmN poly-proline motif (Figures 4, 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo splicing assays shown in Figures 5A–C.

claim: Mutations of residues Tyr454, Asp458, Glu501, Ser468 and Asn483, which are remote from the SmN binding site, had only moderate effects on the activity of RBM5 on FAS splicing.
source: In contrast, mutations of residues, Tyr454, Asp458, Glu501 (Figure 1E) and Ser468 and Asn483 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which are remote from the SmN binding site, had only moderate effects on the activity of RBM5 on FAS splicing.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo splicing assays shown in Figure 1E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Specific recognition of the proline-rich SmN peptide by a cluster of aromatic residues in the RBM5 OCRE domain is required for the function of RBM5 as a splicing regulator.
source: These data further argue that specific recognition of the proline-rich SmN peptide by a cluster of aromatic residues in the RBM5 OCRE domain is required for the function of RBM5 as a splicing regulator.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined mutational and functional analysis shown in Figures 1E, 5, and Table 2.

claim: The knock down of the SmN/B/B' proteins by siRNA in HeLa cells led to an increase in the level of FAS exon 6 skipping in endogenous transcripts or in transcripts derived from a Fas reporter.
source: Consistent with previous results (Saltzman et al., 2011), we observed that the knock down of the SmN/B/B' proteins by siRNA in HeLa cells led to an increase in the level of FAS exon 6 skipping in endogenous transcripts or in transcripts derived from a Fas reporter (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,C).
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,C and citation.

claim: The effects of SmN/B/B' knockdown on FAS exon 6 skipping were attenuated by strengthening FAS exon 6-associated 5' splice site.
source: These effects were attenuated by strengthening FAS exon 6-associated 5' splice site (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), as has been previously reported (Saltzman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and citation.

claim: Co-expression of SmN with a FAS alternative splicing reporter bearing a mutation (Fas U-20C) that increases FAS exon 6 skipping led to increased levels of exon inclusion.
source: Co-expression of SmN with a FAS alternative splicing reporter bearing a mutation (Fas U-20C) that increases FAS exon 6 skipping (Izquierdo et al., 2005), led to increased levels of exon inclusion, while neither expression of the amino terminal part nor of the C-terminal part of the protein did (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and citation.

claim: Expression of SmN variants harboring mutations in the proline-rich stretches (either to glycine or to APAP motif) does not significantly compromise exon inclusion.
source: While expression of SmN variants harboring mutations in the proline-rich stretches (either to glycine or to APAP motif) does not significantly compromise exon inclusion, mutation of the arginines flanking stretches of four prolines does (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Mutation of the arginines flanking stretches of four prolines in SmN compromises exon inclusion.
source: While expression of SmN variants harboring mutations in the proline-rich stretches (either to glycine or to APAP motif) does not significantly compromise exon inclusion, mutation of the arginines flanking stretches of four prolines does (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by splicing assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Three tyrosine residues in the RBM5 OCRE domain (Tyr479, Tyr488 and Tyr495) play crucial roles in the recognition of proline-rich regions present in the conserved C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B'.
source: Taken together, the structural and functional analyses show that three tyrosine residues in the RBM5 OCRE domain (Tyr479, Tyr488 and Tyr495) play crucial roles in the recognition of proline-rich regions present in the conserved C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B' and reveal a tight correlation between this binding and the activity of RBM5 as a regulator of FAS alternative splicing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined structural, biochemical, and functional data presented in Figures 2, 4, 5, and Table 2.

claim: There is a tight correlation between OCRE binding to SmN/B/B' and the activity of RBM5 as a regulator of FAS alternative splicing.
source: Taken together, the structural and functional analyses show that three tyrosine residues in the RBM5 OCRE domain (Tyr479, Tyr488 and Tyr495) play crucial roles in the recognition of proline-rich regions present in the conserved C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B' and reveal a tight correlation between this binding and the activity of RBM5 as a regulator of FAS alternative splicing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined structural, biochemical, and functional data.

claim: The alternative splicing activity of RBM5 depends on the C-terminal region of RBM5.
source: We have previously shown that the alternative splicing activity RBM5 depends on the C-terminal region of RBM5 and that recombinant RBM5 inhibits the transition from the pre-spliceosomal complex A to spliceosomal complex B (Bonnal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Recombinant RBM5 inhibits the transition from the pre-spliceosomal complex A to spliceosomal complex B.
source: We have previously shown that the alternative splicing activity RBM5 depends on the C-terminal region of RBM5 and that recombinant RBM5 inhibits the transition from the pre-spliceosomal complex A to spliceosomal complex B (Bonnal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The inhibition of complex B formation depends on the C-terminal region of RBM5.
source: These and additional transient transfection experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) confirm that the inhibition of complex B formation depends on the C-terminal region of RBM5 and reveal that the OCRE domain is necessary but not sufficient for this activity.
evidence: This is supported by spliceosome assembly assays shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The OCRE domain is necessary but not sufficient for inhibition of complex B formation.
source: These and additional transient transfection experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) confirm that the inhibition of complex B formation depends on the C-terminal region of RBM5 and reveal that the OCRE domain is necessary but not sufficient for this activity.
evidence: This is supported by spliceosome assembly assays shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1,2.

claim: Additional interactions involving the C-terminal region of RBM5 are important for inhibition of complex B formation, including the previously reported interaction with U2AF65.
source: This is consistent with a key role for the interaction of OCRE with the PRM in the spliceosomal tails in the tri-snRNP, but argues that additional interactions involving the C-terminal region of RBM5 are important, including for example the previously reported interaction with U2AF65 (Bonnal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 6 and supported by citation.

claim: The tertiary fold and the mode of PRM recognition by the OCRE domain is distinct from other PRM binding domains, such as GYF, SH3, and WW domains.
source: The tertiary fold and the mode of PRM recognition by the OCRE domain is distinct from other PRM binding domains, such as GYF, SH3, and WW domains (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown by structural comparison in Figure 7A.

claim: Aromatic residues are used to interact with proline residues and to recognize the PPII helix as a common feature among PRM binding domains.
source: Although – as a common feature – aromatic residues are used to interact with proline residues and to recognize the PPII helix (Ball et al., 2005), different secondary structure elements are found in GYF (α-helical), SH3 (α/β fold), WW (β-sheet) and OCRE domains (β-sheet).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and structural comparison.

claim: Different secondary structure elements are found in GYF (α-helical), SH3 (α/β fold), WW (β-sheet) and OCRE domains (β-sheet).
source: Although – as a common feature – aromatic residues are used to interact with proline residues and to recognize the PPII helix (Ball et al., 2005), different secondary structure elements are found in GYF (α-helical), SH3 (α/β fold), WW (β-sheet) and OCRE domains (β-sheet).
evidence: This is shown by structural comparison in Figure 7A and established knowledge.

claim: A PRM motif in the CD2 protein (PPPPGHR) was reported to interact with the GYF domain of the CD2BP2 protein.
source: Interestingly, a somewhat related PRM motif in the CD2 protein (PPPPGHR) was reported to interact with the GYF domain of the CD2BP2 protein (Freund et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The CD2BP2 GYF domain and the FBP21 WW domain have been previously implicated in binding to the PRM sequences of SmB.
source: The CD2BP2 GYF domain and the FBP21 WW domain have been previously implicated in binding to the PRM sequences of SmB, suggesting that interactions between PRMs and these factors may be critical for the function of these proteins in spliceosome regulation (Bedford et al., 1998; Klippel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Interactions between PRMs and CD2BP2 GYF or FBP21 WW domains may be critical for the function of these proteins in spliceosome regulation.
source: The CD2BP2 GYF domain and the FBP21 WW domain have been previously implicated in binding to the PRM sequences of SmB, suggesting that interactions between PRMs and these factors may be critical for the function of these proteins in spliceosome regulation (Bedford et al., 1998; Klippel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: The presence of multiple PRM motifs greatly enhances the overall affinity ranging from KD ≈ mM for a single PRM peptide to KD = 20–40 µM for complete Sm tails.
source: An interesting aspect of the OCRE/Sm interaction is that the presence of multiple PRM motifs greatly enhances the overall affinity ranging from KD ≈ mM for a single PRM peptide to KD = 20–40 µM for complete Sm tails, and thus comparable to other PRM binding domains.
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements shown in Table 2.

claim: The relatively weak affinity of a single PRM found in the Sm tails argues that avidity effects due to the presence of multiple motifs play an important role for high affinity binding.
source: The relatively weak affinity of a single PRM found in the Sm tails argues that avidity effects due to the presence of multiple motifs play an important role for high affinity binding by increasing the local concentration of PRM motifs available for OCRE binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of binding affinities shown in Table 2.

claim: Avidity effects provided by multiple binding sites have also been observed for other PRM binding domains.
source: We note that avidity effects provided by multiple binding sites have also been observed for other PRM binding domains (Varani et al., 2000; Klippel et al., 2011), and that this feature is reminiscent of the recognition of dimethyl-arginine residues in the Sm tails by Tudor domains (Tripsianes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The weak binding affinity of a single motif indicates that the interaction between RBM5 and SmN/B/B' may have been selected to be transient.
source: On the other hand, the weak binding affinity of a single motif indicates that the interaction between RBM5 and SmN/B/B' may have been selected to be transient, as expected for a regulatory interaction that needs to promote interactions with the spliceosome but also needs to be disrupted at later steps of the splicing reaction.
evidence: This is speculation based on the binding affinity data.

claim: The SmN/B/B' tails are intrinsically disordered and extend very far away from the seven-membered Sm core ring in U snRNPs.
source: The fact that the SmN/B/B' tails are intrinsically disordered and extend very far away from the seven-membered Sm core ring in U snRNPs (Figure 7B,C), is consistent with such an activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B,C and is established knowledge.

claim: The recent EM structure of the tri-snRNP revealed that the Sm cores of U4 and U5, as well as the LSm ring of U6 are located at the outside of this large RNP.
source: In fact, the recent EM structure of the tri-snRNP (Nguyen et al., 2015) revealed that the Sm cores of U4 and U5, as well as the LSm ring of U6 are located at the outside of this large RNP (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 7C.

claim: The C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B' of the U4 and U5 components are clearly accessible in the tri-snRNP.
source: Thus, the C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B' of the U4 and U5 components are clearly accessible and could scan for possible binding partners of their proline-rich motifs, such as the RBM5 OCRE domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the EM structure of the tri-snRNP.

claim: The C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B' could scan for possible binding partners of their proline-rich motifs, such as the RBM5 OCRE domain.
source: Thus, the C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B' of the U4 and U5 components are clearly accessible and could scan for possible binding partners of their proline-rich motifs, such as the RBM5 OCRE domain.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural information.

claim: The C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B' could help to localize the tri-snRNP to the splice sites that are regulated by RBM5.
source: This could help to localize the tri-snRNP to the splice sites that are regulated by RBM5.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural and functional data.

claim: SmB was described to participate in alternative splicing of its own pre-mRNA and many additional genes, including the FAS gene.
source: SmB was described to participate in alternative splicing of its own pre-mRNA and many additional genes, including the FAS gene (Saltzman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutations in SmB were linked to cerebro-costo-mandibular syndrome.
source: Recently, mutations in SmB were linked to cerebro-costo-mandibular syndrome (Bacrot et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: RBM5 promotes FAS exon 6 skipping.
source: The multi-domain protein RBM5 promotes FAS exon 6 skipping and it has been proposed that for this activity the protein modulates splice site pairing after the competing 5' and 3' splice sites have been recognized by U1 and U2 snRNPs, respectively (Bonnal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: RBM5 modulates splice site pairing after the competing 5' and 3' splice sites have been recognized by U1 and U2 snRNPs.
source: The multi-domain protein RBM5 promotes FAS exon 6 skipping and it has been proposed that for this activity the protein modulates splice site pairing after the competing 5' and 3' splice sites have been recognized by U1 and U2 snRNPs, respectively (Bonnal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on citation.

claim: RBM5 inhibits the transition from A (U2 snRNP binding) to B (U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP binding) complex formation in the introns flanking exon 6.
source: This model is based upon the observation that RBM5 inhibits the transition from A (U2 snRNP binding) to B (U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP binding) complex formation in the introns flanking exon 6.
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Interactions mediated by the C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B' may facilitate the transition from A to B complex.
source: It is conceivable that interactions mediated by the C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B', which are present in U1, U2 and the tri-snRNP, facilitate the transition from A to B complex and that binding of the OCRE domain of RBM5 prevents these interactions and therefore the progression of spliceosome assembly.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: Binding of the OCRE domain of RBM5 to SmN/B/B' tails may prevent interactions that facilitate the transition from A to B complex and therefore the progression of spliceosome assembly.
source: It is conceivable that interactions mediated by the C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B', which are present in U1, U2 and the tri-snRNP, facilitate the transition from A to B complex and that binding of the OCRE domain of RBM5 prevents these interactions and therefore the progression of spliceosome assembly.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: Direct or indirect association of RBM5 with particular regions of the pre-mRNA may prevent A to B transition of pre-spliceosomes assembled on the flanking introns of exon 6, but fail to prevent tri-snRNP assembly on the distal splice sites, thus facilitating exon skipping.
source: Direct or indirect association of RBM5 with particular regions of the pre-mRNA – likely involving other regions of the protein including RRM or zinc finger domains – may prevent A to B transition of pre-spliceosomes assembled on the flanking introns of exon 6, but fail to prevent tri-snRNP assembly on the distal splice sites, thus facilitating exon skipping.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data and model.

claim: RBM5 interaction with the C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B' may lead to a general decrease in snRNP function, possibly more acute for U2 snRNP.
source: Alternatively, or in addition, RBM5 interaction with the C-terminal tails of SmN/B/B' may lead to a general decrease in snRNP function, possibly more acute for U2 snRNP.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: Decreased activity of U2 snRNP is known to result in increased FAS exon skipping.
source: As decreased activity of U2 snRNP – e.g. by individual knock down of its protein components – is known to result in increased FAS exon skipping (Papasaikas et al., 2015), RBM5-mediated reduction in U2 function could potentially explain at least part of the effects of the protein on FAS splicing regulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: RBM5-mediated reduction in U2 function could potentially explain at least part of the effects of the protein on FAS splicing regulation.
source: As decreased activity of U2 snRNP – e.g. by individual knock down of its protein components – is known to result in increased FAS exon skipping (Papasaikas et al., 2015), RBM5-mediated reduction in U2 function could potentially explain at least part of the effects of the protein on FAS splicing regulation.
evidence: This is speculation based on established knowledge and experimental data.

claim: The OCRE domains of RBM5 and RBM10 are expected to adopt highly similar structures and possibly functions based on primary sequence alignments.
source: It is interesting to note that, based on primary sequence alignments, the OCRE domains of RBM5 and RBM10 are expected to adopt highly similar structures and possibly functions.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence alignments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The recently reported structure of the RBM10 OCRE domain is highly similar to RBM5 OCRE (backbone coordinate r.m.s.d. 1.1Å).
source: In fact, the recently reported structure of the RBM10 OCRE domain is highly similar to RBM5 OCRE (backbone coordinate r.m.s.d. 1.1Å) (Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutation of a conserved tyrosine residue (corresponding to Tyr470 in RBM5) is frequently found associated with lung carcinoma.
source: Interestingly, mutation of a conserved tyrosine residue (corresponding to Tyr470 in RBM5, where it contributes to the recognition of the PRMs by the OCRE domain) is frequently found associated with lung carcinoma (Imielinski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Splicing defects that are linked to impaired interactions with PRM in SmN/B/B' proteins may contribute to the pathogenesis of lung carcinoma.
source: It is thus tempting to speculate that splicing defects that are linked to impaired interactions with PRM in SmN/B/B' proteins contribute to the pathogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural and functional data and the association with lung carcinoma.
